state_priorities.state_summary: 1) The most recent files are GPT's bounded review, finalized on 2 Oct 2026 (commit b8fe78a5, branch codex/sota-review-20261002). In them no new experiment has been launched: SOTA_REVIEW.md:130 says "No experiment has been launched", and CONTINUATION.md:28 says of all five protocols "None ran". I did not check cluster state for 2-16 Oct. 2) The established results are project-reported, and GPT did not reproduce them independently (SOTA_REVIEW.md:9,27). Pruning movements with the learned v8 graph-attention scorer improves fixed-budget bills on larger synthetic cases (40-80 trips) and on the public Hildenbrand and Eberbach cases (E3/E5/E6). E11's full 96-task cohort shows the result repeats across solver seeds: keep .15 wins 23/24 pairs against each baseline and keep .30 wins 24/24, counting a finite bill above a failure. Finite-bill counts are cold 21/24, cold4 9/24, keep .15 23/24 and keep .30 24/24 (SOTA_REVIEW.md:37,41; notes/E11_FULL_COHORT_ANALYSIS.md:13-23). 3) Price support is established only with qualifications. E0 gives tolerance-qualified positive physical-minus-hull gaps on four development timetables, "<= 0.1% of the bill". E9's seeded hull enclosures are tighter on 10/10 cases, but only one hull closes and every large-case gap interval still contains zero (OR_POSITIONING_REVIEW.md:28). 4) Several questions are open. (a) Replay/extraction reliability: 4/6 long Eberbach per-trip runs in E10 fail replay. In E11, an extraction refusal can discard an earlier incumbent, and the 60-s allowance is "not a matched end-to-end cap". (b) Whether learning beats a matched classical greedy rule: E11 has no greedy or random arm. (c) Synthetic-to-public transfer: E7/E8 show reversals, and the public cases have become exploratory. (d) Whether the hull bottleneck is primal columns, pricing lower bounds or price selection. 5) Is the ML model good? GPT's answer is that the scorer is a useful solver-guidance signal (v8 held-out AP 0.843 -> 0.899, log loss 0.0719 -> 0.0543). But that AP gain is "a ranking result, not a bill improvement" (notes/ML_PRIMAL_AND_TRAINING.md:9). Its learned-specific value over cheap classical pruning is unproven, and its gains reverse on public cases when scores are tariff-aware (E7) or keep fractions are aggressive (E8). 6) How to improve it: GPT rejects a bigger or newer network ("Do not pursue first", SOTA_REVIEW.md:202). The sanctioned path has three steps. First, fix extraction and charging repair. Second, make pruning recoverable (predict-and-search or reinsertion, with a valid fallback). Third, only if learned beats greedy, retrain the same architecture on deduplicated, replay-valid, tariff-diverse, cost-weighted topology pools, with economic negatives and one self-improvement cycle that mixes unrestricted, greedy/LP and learned proposals (SOTA_REVIEW.md:61-65; rank 4). 7) Paper status: not ready. The working title "Learning-assisted fleet scheduling with certified price-support bounds" "states an objective, not a result" (SOTA_REVIEW.md:154), and "neither an OR-ready contribution nor an end-to-end speedup is established" (SOTA_REVIEW.md:234). 8) Gerbaux, Desaulniers & Cappart (COR 173, 106848, 2025) already publish learned electric-bus arc pruning and per-trip top-m. The certificate inequalities are "currently elementary" (SOTA_REVIEW.md:183). A viable OR paper therefore needs a fleet-specific coupled-charging mechanism or structural result, matched failure-aware baselines, independent timetables and a decisive economic endpoint. 9) GPT names two fallbacks: a focused scheduling paper if only primal gains survive, or a price-support paper if only the certificates do (SOTA_REVIEW.md:23,189). 10) On "do them": execution is gated. This task forbade runs and file changes, and CONTINUATION.md:9,20,44 requires frozen manifests, mappings, acceptance thresholds and resource accounting before any launch. The first action is the common replay-reliability pipeline (rank 1), then the six-arm learned-versus-classical comparison (rank 2), with rank 3 or rank 5 chosen afterwards by a bottleneck diagnosis. 11) Sealed DEV/TEST/A6/B3/confirmation/GIRO data remain closed, and in any cluster phase EGG yields to v2g*/evspv2g-stochastic jobs.

priorities.name: Reliable topology extraction and charging completion (resolve replay failures, preserve valid incumbents)
priorities.why: E10: 4/6 long Eberbach per-trip runs fail replay, including every 1800-s run. E11: an extraction/projection exception can discard an earlier internal incumbent (notes/E11_INTERPRETATION_REVIEW.md:11). Invalid plans cannot be credited, and every later study shares this pipeline. Four arms: existing extraction; improved scaling with the same tolerances; fixed-route charging repair; scaling plus repair (SOTA_REVIEW.md:142). Effort 24-40 h, plus 8-16 h for an optional exact-LP export. Compute 35-50 CPUh for four arms x three seeds on the existing 30 case/budget cells. Protocol: protocols/NUMERICAL_RELIABILITY_PROTOCOL.md.
priorities.depends_on: None; this is the mandatory foundation. Before intervening, freeze the identities and raw artifacts of all four recorded E10 Eberbach failures; a failed topology may not be dropped from the denominator.
priorities.stop_go: Go: "No accepted plan may fail the original replay; recover ≥90% of the frozen historical failure cohort; median overhead ≤20%." Because the cohort is four runs, ≥90% means all four (SOTA_REVIEW.md:142). Stop: "Stop and reformulate if success requires relaxed reserve/terminal/charger constraints."

priorities.name: Recoverable learned pruning with a classical challenge (six arms)
priorities.why: Tests whether learning earns its cost under a repaired pipeline. Simple widening of the learned ranking is "a recovery baseline, not a nonlearned challenge to the ranking" (FINAL_CONTRIBUTION_CHALLENGE.md:9). Arms: unpruned; current rule; learned widening; full-model predict-and-search; compact reinsertion; matched nonlearned greedy widening. Effort 24-48 h. Compute 45-60 CPUh. Controlling amendment (CONTINUATION.md:29): "six arms, 540 runs, 41.4 estimated solver CPUh, hard 60 CPUh ceiling", superseding the five-arm/50 CPUh design. All arms pay for common fallback acquisition; learned scoring is not charged to arms that don't use it.
priorities.depends_on: Rank 1 (the post-repair pipeline), "subject to freezing the greedy rule".
priorities.stop_go: Go: "≥10% median time-to-quality reduction or ≥1% paired bill improvement over learned widening, with no increased failure rate, a substantive public benefit and no public regression >2%. Separately require useful learned-versus-greedy benefit before broader training." Stop: "Stop if gains disappear after build/repair overhead." If the greedy policy matches learned performance, keep recovery as engineering and "stop treating improved neural labels as the next research priority" (FINAL_CONTRIBUTION_CHALLENGE.md:11).

priorities.name: Separate candidate generation from global pricing certification (oracle allocation)
priorities.why: Learned or restricted solves give pricing upper bounds and columns, but only unrestricted oracles give valid lower bounds. E9's seeded gains do not count seed-acquisition cost. Arms: seeded full pricing; fixed learned/full allocation; adaptive allocation; adaptive allocation plus extra stabilization; and an unseeded full-pricing control with the same total allowance. Effort 20-40 h. Compute 45-55 CPUh for ten cases x three seeds: four seeded policies at 600 s, common seed acquisition up to 900 s, unseeded control at 1,500 s. Measured seed-acquisition cost is charged to each end-to-end algorithm. Protocol: protocols/MATCHED_ORACLE_PROTOCOL.md.
priorities.depends_on: A conditional branch, not a queue item. It follows a bounded bottleneck diagnosis that separates feasible-mixture upper bounds, unrestricted pricing lower bounds and query quality. Choose allocation when both candidate and certification effort show useful marginal returns (SOTA_REVIEW.md:21; FINAL_CONTRIBUTION_CHALLENGE.md:17).
priorities.stop_go: Go: "≥25% reduction in median final hull width, or ≥20% reduction in time to a frozen certificate tolerance, over the strongest matched-budget baseline. All bounds must remain globally valid." Stop: "Stop if a new price policy saves iterations but not end-to-end time."

priorities.name: Tariff-diverse, cost-aware topology pools (training-signal improvement)
priorities.why: Single-incumbent labels confuse "not selected by this solver run" with "undesirable". Arms: single labels vs uniform pools vs cost-weighted pools, with the same architecture and search policy, plus one self-improvement cycle with unrestricted exploration. Effort 24-40 h for the first cycle. Compute 55-70 CPUh: 32 CPUh label collection, a 16.2 CPUh online screen, and a 6.8-21.8 CPUh training/data/replay allowance; any GPU budget is separate. Protocol: protocols/LEARNING_SIGNAL_PROTOCOL.md.
priorities.depends_on: Runs only "if learned guidance earns further investment" (SOTA_REVIEW.md:18), i.e. after rank 2's learned-versus-greedy benefit gate passes.
priorities.stop_go: Go: "≥10% improvement in median primal integral over single labels, paired group benefit and stable public tails/replay. Require uniform-pool ablation." No-go: "AP-only gains or self-confirming omissions are no-go."

priorities.name: Charging-aware route pricing as a full-fleet relaxation (stronger pricing oracle)
priorities.why: Large-case hull gap intervals still contain zero, so stronger unrestricted pricing lower bounds may be needed. The approach builds on resource-extension/backward bounds and shared-capacity dualization (Parmentier; Klein-Schiffer). First prove that every original feasible fleet maps into the route relaxation with a nonincreasing price objective. Effort 60-120 h for a scoped prototype. Compute 20-40 CPUh for an initial pricing-only comparison, "not a full branch-and-price campaign". Normalized error = (V*-ℓ)/max{1,|V*|} with a certified V* (SOTA_REVIEW.md:144). Protocol: protocols/CHARGING_ROUTE_RELAXATION_PROTOCOL.md.
priorities.depends_on: A conditional branch taken after the same bottleneck diagnosis. Prioritize a stronger oracle "when global pricing bounds remain weak despite additional candidate work" (SOTA_REVIEW.md:21).
priorities.stop_go: Go: "On a fixed small cohort with certified references, reduce median normalized lower-bound error ≥20% at a prespecified early checkpoint; on larger cases, reduce time to the same prespecified valid bound ≥25%, including master overhead." Stop: "Stop if the mapping relaxes the wrong model, labels explode, or its bound is too weak to improve E9." Missing references make the gate inconclusive.

contribution_risks: Direct prior art for learned EV-bus pruning: Gerbaux, Desaulniers & Cappart, Computers & Operations Research 173, 106848 (2025), DOI 10.1016/j.cor.2024.106848. It already does GNN arc selection with charging constraints, learns from feasible incumbents, selects the highest-scored incoming and outgoing arcs per trip (Sec. 5.2.4/Alg. 2), combines GNN and greedy arc sets (Sec. 5.3), and runs large-instance/transfer tests. 'No first GNN EV pruning or per-trip top-m claim' (SOTA_REVIEW.md:11; OR_POSITIONING_REVIEW.md:13,28).

Learned warmstarts for certified column generation already exist: Sugishita, Grothey & McKinnon, IJOC 36(4):1129-1146 (2024). Stabilized, inexact and warm-started CG are required baselines, and combining ML with CG is 'not automatically a new method' (OR_POSITIONING_REVIEW.md:15; SOTA_REVIEW.md:95).

Recoverable prediction-guided search is established by Han et al. (ICLR 2023 predict-and-search), Apollo-MILP (ICLR 2025) and learned LNS. 'Novelty cannot be "first uncertainty-guided predict/correct/fix"' (ADAPTIVE_PRUNING_AND_NUMERICS.md:23; SOTA_REVIEW.md:159).

The certificate/bound theory is standard. Weak-duality and Fenchel bounds and cached-price inequalities are 'useful, but currently elementary' (SOTA_REVIEW.md:183). Concavity-based combination of cached bounds has prior art in Geoffrion & Nauss (1977), aggregate-load outer/inner models in Barot-Taylor, Al Taha-Vincent-Bitar and Mukhi-Loho-Abate, and approximate columns with global certificates in Kiwiel-Lemaréchal (SOTA_REVIEW.md:99,116,120).

The unifying insight ('fast operational optimization and fast economic certification require different information') 'is correct but already familiar from decomposition' (FINAL_CONTRIBUTION_CHALLENGE.md:21). Its ingredients are known, so the contribution must be specific structure, analysis and evidence (SOTA_REVIEW.md:163).

No decisive economic endpoint yet. The E0 gaps are small (<= 0.1% of the bill) and only tolerance-qualified, and every large-case physical-minus-hull gap interval contains zero. 'A narrower hull interval is insufficient when the economic conclusion remains unresolved' (SOTA_REVIEW.md:23,165; OR_POSITIONING_REVIEW.md:28).

Weak computational baselines. There is no matched classical/greedy comparator under the repaired pipeline, no matched end-to-end E9 speedup (seed cost precedes the hull budget), and no matched end-to-end cap in E11 (SOTA_REVIEW.md:43; notes/E11_FULL_COHORT_ANALYSIS.md:72).

Evaluation independence is compromised. The public Hildenbrand/Eberbach outcomes helped select models, keep fractions and policies, so they are exploratory. Seeds and tariffs are dependent repeats. E11 covers four correlated progenitor groups. Independent authorized timetables and a frozen final protocol are still needed (SOTA_REVIEW.md:43,146,185).
Reliability: there is 'no demonstrated robust deployment while replay failures persist' (OR_POSITIONING_REVIEW.md:28). Replay rules may not be loosened to erase the failures.

Source-access limits: the de Oliveira-Sagastizábal on-demand-accuracy paper is abstract-only, and Pessoa et al. stabilization was inspected only at abstract level. Convergence guarantees cannot be borrowed for an EGG timeout policy (SOTA_REVIEW.md:23,97,99).

Advancement screens are not contribution gates. Passing the 10%/20%/25% pilot screens on exploratory cases is 'not evidence of a fleet-specific OR contribution'. Each branch needs a named coupled-charging mechanism, its closest comparator and a falsifying outcome (FINAL_CONTRIBUTION_CHALLENGE.md:27-29).

Outcome fork: if only primal gains survive, a focused learning-assisted EV scheduling paper is more coherent. If learning adds little but certificates improve, the stronger paper is a price-support theory/computation paper (SOTA_REVIEW.md:23,189).

ml_quality.verdict: The model works as a movement filter in front of Gurobi. It is not a good planner on its own, and nobody has yet shown that the GNN beats a cheap non-learned ranking. (a) Ranking: on the 20-28-trip bank it ranks well. The v8 attention model's OUTER results are AP 0.899126, log loss 0.054297 and trip-count top-k recall 0.764452, against CatBoost v5 at 0.826484 / 0.069298 / 0.697748 (V8_RESULTS.md:29-32). On the held-out `day` tariff, the v8-equivalent bank2 model drops to AP 0.8278-0.8518 (E4_RESULTS.md:14-17). Ranking was never measured on the scaled or public cases. Used directly as a plan, the learned routes cost +8.60 more than the cold solver (~1.5%) at bank size (E4_RESULTS.md:30). (b) Decisions when pruning: the filter is real and holds up across solver seeds. It beats random pruning 12/12 at 60 s and 300 s, and in the E11 full cohort keep-15% beats cold 20/0/0 when both runs return a plan. But most of the headline 60-s mean gain over cold (-29.369%) comes from making the problem smaller, not from the ranking. Random 30% pruning alone beats cold in the 5/12 cells where cold returns 25-32-bus plans: on 50001:80, cold is +234.70% above the best plan, random +21.30%, learned +9.70%. Where cold works, random is +23.57% to +48.51% and learned is about equal to cold. So the ranking's measurable value is avoiding damage, plus a further ~10-23% bill cut over random on 80-trip cases. The honest effect sizes are the medians: -3.366%/-2.979% in E3 and -6.09%/-6.83% with keep 15% in E6. Nobody has compared the GNN with a slack/deadhead heuristic, a reduced-cost ranking, or the existing CatBoost and logistic rankers. The LP comparison arm is weak: it ranks by x-values, breaks ties by movement index and is charged its solve time. (c) Transfer to public timetables is fragile. Aggressive pruning (keep 5%, top-3 per trip) loses 17-25% on public cases, with the same bill at every budget, which means the pruning removed movements the good plan needs. The tariff-diverse multi8 model is worse on all 6 public cells. (d) The evidence base is small and reused: about 4 synthetic base timetables (each 60-trip case is a prefix of the 80-trip one), 3 public networks, one run per cell outside E11, keep rules tuned on the same cells, and a single model (fold 0/seed 17). Meanwhile E11 shows 10-16% seed-to-seed spread for the learned arms, so single-run differences of a few percent between learned variants are noise.
strengths: In-distribution ranking is strong and still improving with training: v8 attention OUTER log loss 0.054297 / AP 0.899126 / top-k recall 0.764452, against v6 0.071888 / 0.842573 / 0.739570 and CatBoost v5 0.069298 / 0.826484 / 0.697748 (v8-collection/V8_RESULTS.md:29-32). Anchors reproduce v6 exactly (line 11-13).

The scores carry real information beyond random: learned beats random pruning at the same keep rule 15/16 on the bank (~28% of the bill; E3_BANK_RESULTS.md:48,70-71), 12/12 on scaled cases at both budgets (median -24.106% / -24.634%; E3_SCALE_RESULTS.md:44-45), and on every public cell (E5_RESULTS.md:27-29).

The pruning gains survive solver-seed changes in the regime where cold collapses. E11 full cohort: keep 15% vs cold 23/0/1 (both-finite 20/0/0) and keep 30% vs cold 24/0/0 (both-finite 21/0/0) (notes/E11_FULL_COHORT_ANALYSIS.md:13-16). Example: 50000:80 cold 3276.59-3295.46 vs learned keep 15% 887.14-896.06.
Size transfer for pruning: a model trained on 20-28-trip timetables keeps 4-6-bus plans at 80 trips, while cold returns 25-32 buses at 60 s (E3_SCALE_RESULTS.md:57-66).

Transfer at a conservative keep: learned4 at keep 30% is the best arm in 6/6 public cells. It prunes 70% of Eberbach's 10,359 movements, and on Eberbach learned4 at 600 s (1252.17) beats cold at 1800 s (1271.00) (E5_RESULTS.md:51-52,58-66).
The per-trip top-m rule (E10) works without per-regime tuning: m=5 beats cold 27/30 and m=8 beats cold 28/30 (E10_RESULTS.md:47-52).

Downstream value beyond scheduling: seeding the hull computation with learned plans narrows the enclosure width on 10/10 cases (width ratio 0.08-0.63) and newly certifies one case (E9_RESULTS.md:25-28).

Tariff-diverse labels make the routes respond to prices. multi8 improves AP and log loss on the held-out `day` tariff in 4/4 folds and halves the physical gap to cold (+18.19 -> +8.60) (E4_RESULTS.md:14-31).

Cheap and auditable: about 18k parameters, CPU inference, scoring time charged to the learned arm (claude_e3_prune.py), OUTER-fold models on bank cases (claude_score_v8.py:29-37), and failures counted as losses.
weaknesses: (a) Ranking: the labels are single feasible incumbents (2 source fleets per timetable under the source0/source1 tariffs), so equally good alternative movements are trained as negatives. The code itself says 'unselected is not infeasible or suboptimal' (physical_route_graph_v6.py:371). AP therefore measures imitation of one solver trajectory, not schedule quality.

(a) Ranking was only ever measured on the 20-28-trip bank, under the training tariffs or the held-out `day` tariff (bank2 AP 0.8278-0.8518). No ranking or coverage metric exists for the 40-80-trip scaled cases or the public cases where the model is actually used. Top-k recall of 0.764 means ~24% of incumbent edges fall outside the top-(trip count) ranking.

(a) The model is undertrained by design: each epoch accumulates the full-partition gradient and takes one Adam step (physical_route_graph_v6.py:229-243), so 900 epochs = 900 optimizer steps. The selected epoch is within 4 epochs of the cap in 9/12 tasks (V8_RESULTS.md:19-23).

(a) Architecture limits: node states start from mean raw edge features (physical_route_graph_v6.py:161-162). The 'attention' is a softmax against a single learned vector per layer, independent of the receiving node's state (line 127). Two layers reach only 2 hops, there is no global/fleet context, and edge logits are independent, so jointly the predictions need not form a consistent fleet.

(b) Most of the headline gain over cold is problem shrinkage. At 60 s, random 30% pruning alone beats cold in 5/12 scaled cells (all four 80-trip cells and 50001:60, i.e. exactly where cold returns 25-32 buses). Examples: 50000:80 cold 263.12% vs random 32.55% vs learned 2.15%; 50003:80 cold 307.85% vs random 31.45% vs learned 4.19% (E3_SCALE_RESULTS.md:14-25). The 80-trip bills go cold -> random -> learned: 3271 -> 1194 -> 920; 4082 -> 1479 -> 1338; 4499 -> 1618 -> 1306; 3872 -> 1248 -> 989 (lines 59-65). Shrinkage cuts the bill ~64-68%; ranking adds a further ~10-23%.

(b) Where the unpruned solver works, the model adds about nothing: the bank's learned4 vs cold4 is a wash at 5/5/6 (E3_BANK_RESULTS.md:50-51). At 40 trips all keep settings are within ~2% of cold (E6_RESULTS.md:69). Pruning-induced losses do occur: 10072 +0.33% and 10078 +0.09% (the pruning removed a movement the best plan uses), 50002:60 +8.36% at 300 s, and 10068 extraction refusals.

(b) Pruning decisions are very sensitive to how much is kept. On 50001:80 at 60 s, keep 5/10/15/30/50% gives +0.48% / +11.07% / +2.74% / +91.61% / +183.93% (E8_RESULTS.md:21), and in E11 keep 30% on that case has median 2035.87 vs 1116.77 at keep 15%. The best fraction tracks how many movements the solver can handle in the time budget, which again points to shrinkage.
(b) Reliability: per-trip pruning on Eberbach failed exact replay in 4/6 runs, including every 1800-s run, vs 0/10 for global-fraction runs (E10_RESULTS.md:58-64).

(c) Coverage fails off-distribution: on public cases, keep 5% is +17.58%/+17.86% on Eberbach and +18.50% on Hildenbrand 16, and m=3 is +24.64% on Eberbach (E8_RESULTS.md:62-67; E10_RESULTS.md:12-13). The bills are identical across budgets (e.g. 625.77 at both 180 s and 600 s; Hildenbrand 15 505.00/505.00), so the pruned model solves fast and the loss is pure ranking/coverage error.

(c) Tariff-diverse training does not transfer: multi8 is worse than v8 on all 6 public cells (+0.31% to +5.25%) and only 16/14 overall (median -0.01%) (E7_RESULTS.md:9-14,40). Even v8 runs on the `day` tariff, which it never trained on (E4_RESULTS.md:7-8).

(c) The features cannot represent the public domain shift. The synthetic generator has only places A, B and depot D (claude_scale_cases.py:54-66). The 17 features (learned_proposals.py:19-24) have no separate deadhead travel time/distance (only `same_place`; idle wait is folded into `duration`/`movement_energy`), no charger power or connector count, and no vehicle or deadhead cost. Scaled cases change charger power with size (90*ceil(services/28) kW, claude_scale_cases.py:9,36) and public cases have one 360 kW connector with 400 kWh buses, but the model never sees charger power.

(d) There is no cheap non-learned ranking control. The LP arm ranks by x-values of the linear-price relaxation, breaks ties at x=0 by movement index (claude_e3_prune.py:78,85), and movements are generated in before-trip order (claude_scale_cases.py:67-68), so beyond the LP support it keeps an index-ordered filler, not a ranking. It is also charged ~100 s on Eberbach (E5_RESULTS.md:70-71). The existing CatBoost v5 and logistic EdgePrior (learned_proposals.py:170-205) were never run through the pruning harness. GPT's FINAL_CONTRIBUTION_CHALLENGE.md §1 makes the same point.

(d) The cold baseline is single-thread Gurobi with no warm start and no constructive incumbent. Its 25-32-bus plans at 80 trips are a first-incumbent failure that a classical construction (min-bus assignment + charging LP) or heuristic-focused solver settings might also fix. The large mean gains are measured against that weak baseline.

(d) Correlated and reused instances: 60-trip cases are prefixes of the same-ID 80-trip cases, giving 4 independent synthetic base timetables, not 8 or 12 (E11_INTERPRETATION_REVIEW.md:5; E11_FULL_COHORT_ANALYSIS.md:72). Public cases are 3 networks (Hildenbrand 15/16 are two depots of one network), and the two budgets are correlated observations (Hildenbrand 16 learned4 528.06 at both 180 s and 600 s). The same cells were reused in E3/E6/E7/E8/E10/E11 to choose keep rules, and the v1->v8 lineage was selected on the same 128-group bank (V8_RESULTS.md:35-36).

(d) Single runs and a single model: E3-E10 use one run per cell and one scoring model (fold 0 / seed 17; claude_score_v8.py:31-32). E11 seed spreads are learned keep 30% on 50002:80 1205.60-1402.53 (~16%), keep 15% on 50001:60 888.42-981.63 (~10.5%), and cold on 50003:80 1280.97-3857.75 (3x) (E11_FULL_COHORT_ANALYSIS.md:43,52,61). E7's single-run differences are therefore not distinguishable from noise. There is no seed replication on any public case and no model-seed variance on decisions.

(d) Comparisons are against 'the best bill found by any arm' (mostly learned arms), not an optimum. E9's D intervals at 60-80 trips are tens to hundreds of units wide (e.g. 50003:80 [723.17, 955.08]), so distance to optimal is unknown.

improvements.idea: 1. Zero-solver offline diagnostics from saved outputs: for every scaled/public case, compute per-trip recall@m (m = 1..8), recall at keep 5/15/30%, and whole-plan coverage (does the pruned set contain every movement of a reference plan?). Do this for v8, the 12 v8 fold/seed models, CatBoost v5, the logistic EdgePrior and a slack/deadhead heuristic. Correlate with the bill losses observed in E3-E10.
improvements.rationale: Decision quality for pruning is a coverage question, yet no coverage metric exists at the sizes and domains where the model is used. The identical-across-budget public losses (keep 5%, m=3) and bank 10072/10078 show coverage failure directly. Saved `e3.json` rows contain the `movements` of each plan (claude_e3_prune.py), so this needs no new solves. Caveat: best-known plans often come from learned arms, which biases coverage toward v8; also use cold-found plans (40-trip cold, Eberbach cold 1800 s 1271.00) and report both.
improvements.expected_impact: High information per cost. Shows whether the GNN's AP lead over CatBoost (0.899 vs 0.826) survives the per-trip floor and top-m decode, sets the per-trip m needed for coverage on public cases, and screens which heuristic ranker is worth running in #2.
improvements.cost: ~0.5-1 day of analysis; ~0 solver CPU-h (inference only).

improvements.idea: 2. Ranking-source ablation in the existing pruning harness (claude_e3_prune.py): v8 vs CatBoost v5 vs logistic EdgePrior vs a frozen slack/deadhead/depot-access greedy ranking vs an LP reduced-cost ranking (not x-values with index tie-breaks) vs random. Use the same rules (m=5, m=8, keep 15%), the same round policy (learned4-style), 3 solver seeds, and include public cases. Also add a stronger unpruned baseline (constructive min-bus warm start or heuristic-focused Gurobi settings).
improvements.rationale: This is the missing causal control. Random pruning is a straw man, and the LP arm is degraded by index tie-breaking and charged solve time. If a slack heuristic plus the per-trip floor matches v8 within ~1% median, most of the benefit is problem shrinkage plus common sense, and investment in neural labels should stop (GPT FINAL_CONTRIBUTION_CHALLENGE §1 and RECOVERABLE_PRUNING_PROTOCOL arm 6 already require a nonlearned greedy arm).
improvements.expected_impact: Decides whether improving the GNN is worth anything. A plausible outcome is that heuristic rankers match v8 on synthetic A/B/D cases (very regular structure) but not on public geometry. That would localize the model's value to transfer, where it is weakest.
improvements.cost: ~1 day of engineering. Estimate for 12 scaled cells x (60+300 s) + 3 public cases x 2 budgets, x 3 seeds x 4 new arms: ~28 solver CPU-h (~10 CPU-h for a one-budget subset).

improvements.idea: 3. Recovery around pruning: (i) solve the pruned MIP, then warm-start the full or widened MIP from its replay-valid plan for the remaining budget; (ii) staged, trip-coherent reinsertion of excluded movements on stagnation or infeasibility; (iii) a Hamming trust region sum(e in S0) x_e <= Delta (predict-and-search). Keep the accepted incumbent outside the solver.
improvements.rationale: The losses of the current rule are irrevocable-deletion errors (public keep 5% / m=3, 50002:60 +8.36%, bank 10072/10078, 10068 refusals). The 'warm-start full MIP from pruned plan' remedy proposed in E3 finding 3 was never run. With recovery, aggressive keep sets (which win at 80 trips: keep 5% within 0.03-2.03%) can be used everywhere without regime tuning.
improvements.expected_impact: Removes most of the 17-25% public tail at tight keep and the single-digit synthetic losses, giving a safe anytime pipeline. GPT's go gate is >=10% median time-to-quality or >=1% median bill vs simple widening, with no public regression >2%. Note that full-model trust regions may save little build/charging work on Eberbach (10,359 movements).
improvements.cost: GPT's six-arm protocol: 540 runs, ~41.4 solver CPU-h, 60 CPU-h ceiling; ~16-28 h implementation (ML_PRIMAL_AND_TRAINING.md priority 1).
improvements.evidence_or_source: E3_SCALE_RESULTS.md:77-80; E8_RESULTS.md:71-80; notes/RECOVERABLE_PRUNING_REVIEW.md; protocols/RECOVERABLE_PRUNING_PROTOCOL.md:11-20,46,54; Han et al. ICLR 2023 (ML2)

improvements.idea: 4. Adaptive per-trip decoding from an ensemble: average the 12 existing v8 models (4 folds x 3 seeds) instead of only fold 0/seed 17. For each trip side, keep candidates until a cumulative per-trip probability mass (top-p) is reached, and widen m where models disagree (an out-of-distribution signal). Keep the >=3 floor.
improvements.rationale: E8 shows the right keep depends on regime (keep 5% best at 80 synthetic trips, keep 30% best on public), and E10 shows m=3 fails on public but m=5/8 are robust. Model disagreement and per-trip probability mass should flag exactly the trips where the ranking is unreliable. claude_score_v8.py:31-32 uses only task 0 for scaled/public, so the ensemble costs nothing to train.
improvements.expected_impact: Medium. Should recover most of the m=3/keep-5% public losses while keeping small kept sets on synthetic cases. There is no coverage guarantee under shift; it is a heuristic control (ML_PRIMAL_AND_TRAINING.md:114).
improvements.cost: ~0.5 day of code; scoring is seconds; evaluation ~10-20 solver CPU-h if it shares the #2 grid.

improvements.idea: 5. Training objective and optimization fixes: (i) replace per-edge BCE with a per-trip listwise softmax loss over each trip's incoming candidates and over its outgoing candidates (every plan picks exactly one of each), optionally plus BCE; (ii) take minibatch Adam steps (~32 steps per epoch at 8 graphs per batch) with an LR schedule instead of one step per epoch; (iii) select checkpoints by per-trip recall@m or coverage on inner groups, not inner log loss (physical_route_graph_v6.py:253); (iv) weight positives up, since pruning only pays for false negatives.
improvements.rationale: The decoder actually used (per-trip top-m, plus the floor under global keep) is a per-trip ranking decision, but the loss is symmetric global BCE. The optimizer took only 900 steps, with selected epochs at the cap. ConPaS (ICML 2024) warns that accuracy/AUROC need not predict search performance, so selection must move toward the decision metric.
improvements.expected_impact: Moderate and uncertain: higher per-trip recall at small m makes small kept sets safer, especially combined with #4. Judge by replay-valid bill and time-to-quality in the #2 grid, not by AP.
improvements.cost: ~1 day of code; retraining ~7.5 CPU-h per 12-task fold/seed sweep at the V8 scale (V8_RESULTS.md:3-5), less with fewer epochs needed.

improvements.idea: 6. Features and architecture for transfer: add size-invariant competition features (rank and z-score of slack/energy among the before-trip's outgoing and the after-trip's incoming candidates; number of feasible alternatives), and separate deadhead travel time/energy from idle time. Add charger features: per_bus_kw, connectors, recharge potential = window x power / battery. Add vehicle_cost and deadhead_cost_per_min, a global context node (fleet-size proxy, time-binned charger contention), and attention that depends on the receiving node.
improvements.rationale: The current features cannot express what differs on public networks (many terminals, deadhead geometry, one 360 kW connector, 400 kWh buses). Scaled cases silently change charger power with size. Mean aggregation over complete-ish trip graphs dilutes as size grows, whereas explicit rank features match the top-m decision and are size-invariant.
improvements.expected_impact: Medium for public transfer, small in-distribution. It mostly matters together with #7 (public-like training data); feature changes cannot teach geometry the generator never shows.
improvements.cost: ~1-2 days of code; retraining ~7.5 CPU-h; evaluation shares the #2/#4 grid.

improvements.idea: 7. Data and labels: (i) a public-like synthetic generator (many terminals, a realistic deadhead matrix, 37-105 services, 400 kWh / single 360 kW connector, mixed tariffs); (ii) labels at 40-80+ trips from long or recovery-enabled solves (a size curriculum); (iii) pools of several replay-valid, deduplicated topologies per timetable, with cost-weighted soft positives, so alternative good movements are not trained as negatives; (iv) at most one relabel cycle that also includes unpruned/random collection arms, to avoid self-confirming omissions.
improvements.rationale: Today's 256 label graphs come from 128 small A/B/D timetables. Single-incumbent labels make 'unselected' noisy. E7 shows that adding tariff diversity alone does not transfer to public cases, so the shift is topological/physical, not tariff-driven (E1: bus count never changes across tariffs).
improvements.expected_impact: The largest potential lever for public transfer and for coverage at small m. Highest cost, and it must be evaluated on public networks never used for tuning.
improvements.cost: Generator ~2-4 days. GPT's pool-label pilot ~55-70 CPU-h (32 TRAIN timetables x 4 tariffs x 3 arms x 300 s = 32 solver CPU-h + evaluation 16.2 + training). Size-curriculum labels add roughly 600 s x N timetables.

improvements.idea: 8. Evaluation protocol fixes, applied to every item above: >=10-20 independent synthetic base timetables per size (no prefix pairs); 3 solver seeds including public cases; >=3 model seeds/folds; public networks never used for keep/m selection held out as the test (the current 3 are now development data); report time-to-quality or primal-integral curves, success denominators and failure classes, alongside median and 90th-percentile paired differences grouped by base timetable. Fix the replay/charge-projection numerics first so failures do not dominate the comparisons.
improvements.rationale: The current effective sample is ~4 synthetic base timetables + 3 public networks, reused across E3-E11 to choose rules, with one run per cell and up to 16% seed spread. Means are driven by cold collapse. Replay refusals hit the pruned arms (E10 Eberbach 4/6) and the extraction path can drop earlier valid plans (E11_INTERPRETATION_REVIEW.md:11).
improvements.expected_impact: Without it, none of #2-#7 can be credited. With it, the claim becomes 'learned pruning (+ recovery) beats unpruned and heuristic-pruned solving by X% median on unseen networks'.
improvements.cost: Engineering ~1-2 days (generator seeds, summarizer with failure-aware pairing, already prototyped in E11_FULL_COHORT_ANALYSIS); compute scales with the grid, ~30-60 solver CPU-h for a screening grid; numerical-reliability study per GPT protocol.

papers.citation: Juliette Gerbaux, Guy Desaulniers, Quentin Cappart. "A machine-learning-based column generation heuristic for electric bus scheduling." Computers & Operations Research 173 (2025) 106848. DOI 10.1016/j.cor.2024.106848 (resolves to Elsevier PII S0305054824003204). Received 20 Jan 2024, accepted 8 Sep 2024, available online 25 Sep 2024. Open access CC BY-NC. Preprint: GERAD G-2024-13.
papers.what_they_do: I read the full 14-page published PDF. Its embedded metadata gives DOI 10.1016/j.cor.2024.106848, and Crossref confirms the record. PROBLEM: the multi-depot electric vehicle scheduling problem (MDEVSP), with a piecewise-linear charging function of three pieces (1539.7, 716.0 and 240.5 Wh/min), capacitated charging stations (at most u_h buses charging at once), 15-min charging periods, a 100 kWh battery, and optional depot returns. COST (§3.1, Table 1): fixed cost c_F=1000 per bus, waiting cost c_W=2/min, deadhead cost, c_R=30 per depot return and c_H=30 per charge event. There is NO electricity/energy price term, and grepping the text finds no 'price', 'tariff' or 'energy cost'. WHAT IS LEARNED (§5.2): a GNN following the Joshi et al. 2022 formalization (L=25 layers, p=128) outputs the probability that each arc is in 'a good-quality MDEVSP solution obtained with the basic CG heuristic'. This is imitation of heuristic incumbents. Training uses weighted BCE (weight 1 on positive arcs, 0.1 on negatives), Adam with lr 1e-4, batch size 5, a 70/15/15 split and ROC >0.95. Features (Table B.7) are 9+2n_L per vertex and 8 per arc: cost, energy, deadhead time, waiting time, elapsed time, departure-time ranks and cost rank. None of them is a price. WHAT IS PRUNED: only the 'selectable' arcs (trip-trip connections, to/from-station and to/from-depot). Pull-out/pull-in, charging and idle arcs are always kept. Algorithm 2 (§5.2.4, p.7-8) keeps, for each trip vertex, the n_A highest-probability outgoing and the n_A highest-probability incoming selectable arcs, and takes the union. A greedy constructive heuristic (Alg. 1, with an optional randomized variant n_R, n_S) is the second selector. The hybrid (§5.3) is the union of the greedy and GNN arc sets. The reduced network is built ONCE before column generation, with no reinsertion or recovery. HOW THE REDUCED PROBLEM IS SOLVED: the reduced arc set restricts the SPPRC pricing networks inside a column-generation diving heuristic (Gencol, CPLEX 20.1, single thread, with coverage perturbation and early CG termination). It is not a compact MILP. INSTANCES: Montreal lines (Brasseur 2022 generator). Subsets A-F have 568-1474 trips; subset G averages 2600 trips (range 2374-3115), and only 35 G instances were used for training. The instances are public at gerad.ca/~guyd/mdevsp.html. RESULTS: the abstract reports 71.6% average time reduction with +2.2% cost over 405 instances, and on 8 larger instances 52.5% time saving at a 4.2% gap via transfer learning (E then G). Table 4 (subset A, cgBasic 454.2 s): cgGNN(A,1) cuts time 97.7% but raises cost +161.3%; cgGNN(A,2) gives 80.1% / +12.4%; cgGNN(A,3) gives 57.2% / +1.6%; cgGRD(3,3) gives 80.9% / +8.2%; cgRND(2) gives 88.6% / +111.4%; cgHBD(A,2,1,1) gives 70.8% / +1.4%; and the oracle cgUtopic gives 99.1% / 0.0%. Table 6: training on E only and applying to G gives +40.6% cost. Industrial partner and funder: GIRO Inc.
papers.overlap_with_egg: Direct and close. EGG's E10 rule (E10_RESULTS.md line 4: 'keep each trip's m best incoming and m best outgoing direct/depot movements'; PROTOCOL.md line 6: 'plus all pullouts/pullins') is essentially Gerbaux's Algorithm 2 with always-kept non-selectable arcs. EGG's labels are 'imitation of feasible incumbents' (GPT_HANDOFF_20261002.md line 93), the same supervision Gerbaux uses. The fragility of tight learned-only keep sets is also shared: Gerbaux's cgGNN(A,1) has +161.3% cost, and EGG's E10 m=3 has +18.5% on Hildenbrand 16 and +24.6% on Eberbach. Gerbaux already answers that fragility with a greedy-union hybrid that EGG has never run. Scale and transfer: Gerbaux works at 568-3115 trips, while EGG's largest public case is Eberbach with 105 services and 10,359 movements, so EGG cannot claim scale or transfer novelty. Real differences: EGG prunes a compact path-flow MILP with continuous time-indexed charging solved directly by Gurobi, rather than CG pricing networks. EGG's objective includes time-varying energy prices and a quadratic aggregate supply cost, and its scorer has window-price features. These are model/implementation variants, not a new pruning principle. GPT's characterization (SOTA_REVIEW.md line 11; OR_POSITIONING_REVIEW.md line 13; EV_PRICING_AND_HULL.md line 17) is accurate. GPT did not note the missing energy-price term, the GNN-only failure rows, or the GIRO link: EGG's sealed data include private GIRO data (GPT_HANDOFF line 75).

papers.citation: Nagisa Sugishita, Andreas Grothey, Ken McKinnon. "Use of Machine Learning Models to Warmstart Column Generation for Unit Commitment." INFORMS Journal on Computing 36(4):1129-1146 (2024; Crossref issued 2024-07). DOI 10.1287/ijoc.2022.0140. Author manuscript arXiv:2110.06872 (v1 13 Oct 2021; v2 15 Dec 2023).
papers.what_they_do: I verified the bibliographic record through Crossref and read the full arXiv v2 manuscript. The publisher page returned 403. WHAT IS LEARNED: initial dual values for the system-wide load-balance and spinning-reserve constraints in a Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition of unit commitment (UC). The master problem replaces each X_g by conv(X_g) (eq. 2.2, p.5). The models are k-NN (k=4), a random forest, and a neural network (4 hidden layers of 1000 units, skip connections, tanh). The network is trained either by regression on optimal duals ('single-sampling') or by directly maximizing the expected Lagrangian dual bound ('double-sampling', 24 h on 8 CPU cores). The predicted duals become the centre of a quadratically regularized restricted master problem, and the paper says the regularization is 'crucial'. NOTHING IS PRUNED: pricing stays exact per generator, so bounds remain valid. INSTANCES: 200, 600 and 1000 generators (Borghetti et al. data, UK demand), 100 test instances per size, with only the demand varying. RESULTS: Table 2, 1000 generators, initial bound gap (lb_CPLEX minus lb1): coldstart 99.882, LP relaxation (LPR) 0.092, column pre-population 0.073, double-sampling network 0.026. Table 4 (with primal heuristic), 1000 generators at 0.25% tolerance: CPLEX 600.0 s (0 solved), coldstart 590.0 s (15 solved), LPR 131.2 s, column pre-population 112.6 s, double-sampling network 65.9 s. The paper never uses the phrase 'convex hull pricing'. Mathematically, though, its D-W dual bound is the Lagrangian/convex-hull relaxation, and the duals it warm-starts are the convex-hull price vector of that UC model.
papers.overlap_with_egg: This is a stronger threat to E9 and to Protocol 3 than GPT stated. Learned warm starts for the very D-W computation that yields convex-hull prices are published. EGG's E9 mechanism (learned primal plans as seed columns: GPT_HANDOFF line 43) is one of Sugishita's BASELINES, 'column pre-population', and learned duals beat it at tight tolerance on the 600- and 1000-generator instances. GPT's citation (IJOC 36(4):1129-1146, 2024; SOTA_REVIEW.md line 95) is correct. Differences: Sugishita's blocks are many small independent per-generator MILPs, while EGG has one hard coupled complete-fleet pricing oracle. Sugishita targets a UC solution with a suboptimality bound, not price-support certification or physical-minus-hull gaps.

papers.what_they_do: I verified this through Crossref and the arXiv abstract page; I did not read the full text in this pass. The method is applied to vehicle and crew scheduling in public transit and to VRPTW, with time reductions 'of up to 40%'. GPT's note (EV_PRICING_AND_HULL.md line 22) says, from the author PDF, that the method switches to the complete graph when too few columns are found and terminates with full-network pricing. I did not independently re-check that detail.
papers.overlap_with_egg: This is the generic precedent for learned network reduction in transit scheduling, and the source of the heuristic-then-full-pricing pattern. It directly anticipates any EGG 'learned restricted oracle plus full certifying oracle' design (Protocol 3). It is not EV-specific and has no charging.

papers.citation: Mouad Morabit, Guy Desaulniers, Andrea Lodi. "Machine-Learning-Based Column Selection for Column Generation." Transportation Science 55(4):815-831 (2021). DOI 10.1287/trsc.2021.1045. GERAD G-2020-29 (May 2020).
papers.what_they_do: I verified this through Crossref and the GERAD record and abstract; I did not read the full text. A learned model selects a subset of the columns generated at each CG iteration, to cut restricted-master reoptimization time. It is tested on vehicle and crew scheduling and on VRPTW, with generalization across sizes and gains 'up to 30%'.
papers.overlap_with_egg: Low. It addresses master-problem time, whereas EGG's bottleneck is the single complete-fleet pricing oracle. GPT's distinction from the arc-selection paper (SOTA_REVIEW.md line 89) is correct.

papers.citation: Qingyu Han, Linxin Yang, Qian Chen, Xiang Zhou, Dong Zhang, Akang Wang, Ruoyu Sun, Xiaodong Luo. "A GNN-Guided Predict-and-Search Framework for Mixed-Integer Linear Programming." ICLR 2023. arXiv:2302.05636 (v4 6 Mar 2023; journal-ref 'ICLR2023').
papers.what_they_do: I verified this from the arXiv abstract page; the venue comes from the journal-ref field. A GNN predicts marginal probabilities for the binaries. The method then searches a trust region that allows a bounded number of disagreements with the fixed predictions, rather than hard-fixing them. The paper reports '51.1% and 9.9%' primal-gap improvements over SCIP and Gurobi.
papers.overlap_with_egg: Generic. EGG's hard movement pruning is the zero-disagreement special case. Any 'recoverable pruning' claim (Protocol 2) is anticipated at the generic MILP level.

papers.citation: Taoan Huang, Aaron M. Ferber, Arman Zharmagambetov, Yuandong Tian, Bistra Dilkina. "Contrastive Predict-and-Search for Mixed Integer Linear Programs." ICML 2024, PMLR 235:19757-19771.
papers.what_they_do: I verified this on the PMLR proceedings page (abstract only). The method trains with contrastive learning, using high-quality solutions as positives and low-quality or infeasible ones as negatives. It then predicts and fixes a subset of the integer variables and solves the reduced MILP.
papers.overlap_with_egg: This is generic prior art for EGG's planned cost-aware or solution-pool training (Protocol 4, E4 labels). Training on pools of solutions with negatives is not novel.

papers.citation: Haoyang Liu, Jie Wang, Zijie Geng, Xijun Li, Yuxuan Zong, Fangzhou Zhu, Jianye Hao, Feng Wu. "Apollo-MILP: An Alternating Prediction-Correction Neural Solving Framework for Mixed-Integer Linear Programming." ICLR 2025. arXiv:2503.01129 (3 Mar 2025; journal-ref ICLR 2025).
papers.what_they_do: I verified this from the arXiv abstract page and its journal-ref; fetching proceedings.iclr.cc failed. The method alternates prediction with a trust-region correction that produces a reference solution. It fixes only the variables with low uncertainty under an Uncertainty-based Error upper BOund (UEBO), and reports 'over a 50% reduction in the solution gap'.
papers.overlap_with_egg: Generic prior art for iterative or recoverable fixing and widening around predictions. It anticipates the mechanism, though not a fleet- or charging-specific policy.

papers.citation: Jun Kang Yap, Vishnu Monn Baskaran, Wen Shan Tan, Ze Yang Ding, Hao Wang, David L. Dowe. "Joint Optimisation of Electric Vehicle Routing and Scheduling: A Deep Learning-Driven Approach for Dynamic Fleet Sizes." arXiv:2507.15307 (21 Jul 2025); comments field: 'Accepted at International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN 2025)'.
papers.what_they_do: I verified the arXiv abstract page. The IJCNN venue comes only from the comments field. A CNN predicts the binary variables of a day-ahead MIP that jointly covers EV routing, charging, discharging and generator scheduling. Confident predictions are fixed and the solver finds the rest. A padding mechanism handles a varying number of EVs. The case study uses the IEEE 33-bus system and the Nguyen-Dupuis network, and reports '97.8%' runtime reduction, '99.5% feasibility' and less than '0.01%' deviation from optimal.
papers.overlap_with_egg: This answers the question of whether 2024-2026 work does predict-and-fix for EV scheduling with charging and grid costs: yes. It is not timetabled bus-fleet scheduling (no trip-coverage network) and it involves no price-support certification. It weakens any 'first learned solution reduction for EV charging/routing MILPs' claim.

papers.citation: Francesco Demelas, Joseph Le Roux, Mathieu Lacroix, Axel Parmentier. "Predicting Lagrangian Multipliers for Mixed Integer Linear Programs." ICML 2024, PMLR 235:10368-10384. arXiv:2310.14659.
papers.what_they_do: I verified this on the PMLR page (abstract). A GNN encoder-decoder predicts the Lagrangian multipliers of relaxed constraints, trained by directly maximizing the resulting Lagrangian bound. On multi-commodity network design and generalized assignment it 'closes up to 85% of the gap' between the continuous relaxation and the best Lagrangian bound, and it warm-starts descent methods.
papers.overlap_with_egg: Generic learned Lagrangian, and hence convex-hull, dual prediction. The bounds it produces are valid by construction. Together with Sugishita, it means 'learned prices that give valid bounds' cannot be EGG's novelty.

papers.citation: Mathieu Tanneau, Pascal Van Hentenryck. "Dual Lagrangian Learning for Conic Optimization." arXiv:2402.03086 (v1 5 Feb 2024; v2 24 May 2024). NeurIPS 2024 per the conference listing seen only in search results.
papers.what_they_do: I verified the arXiv abstract page; the NeurIPS venue is not verified from a primary record. The method learns dual-feasible proxies, using dual completion and conic projection layers, so its outputs give valid Lagrangian dual bounds for conic programs. It reports '1000x speedups' over interior-point solvers with gaps 'under 0.5%'.
papers.overlap_with_egg: Adjacent. It establishes learned certificates with guaranteed validity for convex programs. EGG's Fenchel/convex-hull bounds from pricing MILPs are a different, nonconvex setting.

papers.citation: Yunzhuang Shen, Yuan Sun, Xiaodong Li, Zhiguang Cao, Andrew Eberhard, Guangquan Zhang. "Adaptive Stabilization Based on Machine Learning for Column Generation." ICML 2024. arXiv:2405.11198 (18 May 2024; 'Accepted by ICML'24').
papers.what_they_do: I verified the arXiv abstract page. The method uses an ML prediction of the optimal CG duals plus an adaptive stabilization that exploits the prediction, and shows faster convergence on graph coloring.
papers.overlap_with_egg: It anticipates 'learned duals plus stabilization' in Protocol 3.

papers.citation: Puja Sarkar, Vivekanand B. Khanapuri, Manoj Kumar Tiwari. "Accelerating the stabilized column generation using machine learning." Computers & Industrial Engineering 200 (2025) 110837. DOI 10.1016/j.cie.2024.110837.
papers.what_they_do: Only the bibliographic record is verified, via Crossref. The content comes from a search-engine summary only: ML predicts optimal duals or the configuration for stabilized CG, tested on workforce scheduling. I have not seen the abstract or full text from a primary source.
papers.overlap_with_egg: Further crowding of learned-dual stabilization for CG. Low direct overlap.

papers.citation: Olivia Wang, Reem Khir. "Learning to Control Stabilization in Column Generation." arXiv:2604.23889 (v1 26 Apr 2026; v2 6 May 2026).
papers.what_they_do: I verified the arXiv abstract page. The paper gives a common framework for smoothing and penalization stabilization, with parameter bounds, an analysis of predicted duals used as reference points, and convergence guarantees. Its method, RLSCG, uses reinforcement learning to set the stabilization parameters at each iteration. Experiments are on cutting stock.
papers.overlap_with_egg: It anticipates learned or adaptive stabilization with convergence guarantees. Any EGG 'adaptive allocation' theorem must go beyond this.

papers.citation: Zhengzhong Ricky You, Bo Tang, Haoran Liu, Baichuan Mo. "Learned Pairwise Deep Dual-Optimal Inequalities for Stabilizing Column Generation." arXiv:2607.13373 (15 Jul 2026).
papers.what_they_do: I verified the arXiv abstract page. The method predicts pairwise orderings between dual variables and adds them to the master problem as dual-optimal inequalities. Reported results: on CVRP, an 89.7% geometric-mean reduction in root CG time with 1.3% mean bound loss; on VRPTW, 93.9% with 0.5% loss. A recovery procedure keeps the speedup while 'guaranteeing no CG bound loss'.
papers.overlap_with_egg: This is the dual-side analogue of EGG's 'recoverable pruning with a valid fallback'. It constrains the novelty of a 'learned acceleration with a certified recovery' claim for CG bounds.

papers.citation: Abdo Abouelrous, Laurens Bliek, Adriana F. Gabor, Yaoxin Wu, Yingqian Zhang. "Reinforcement Learning for Solving the Pricing Problem in Column Generation: Applications to Vehicle Routing." arXiv:2504.02383 (v1 3 Apr 2025; v2 19 Aug 2025; journal submission).
papers.what_they_do: I verified the arXiv abstract page. An attention-based RL model solves the CG pricing problem end to end for a VRP variant. It reaches a 'reasonable objective gap' for the LP relaxation faster than a DP heuristic.
papers.overlap_with_egg: Low. It is a heuristic learned oracle, so it gives no valid bound and could not replace EGG's certifying global pricing.

papers.citation: Xenia Haslinger, Elisabeth Gaar, Sophie N. Parragh. "An exact approach for the multi-depot electric vehicle scheduling problem." arXiv:2504.13063 (v1 17 Apr 2025; v2 6 Nov 2025).
papers.what_they_do: I verified the arXiv abstract page. It presents 3-index and 2-index MILPs (the latter solved by branch-and-cut) for the MDEVSP with partial charging. The objective is lexicographic (fleet size, then charging stops, then energy), and the instances have up to 80 service trips. The abstract mentions no ML and no electricity price.
papers.overlap_with_egg: None on ML. It is relevant as an exact non-ML method at EGG's synthetic scale of 40-80 trips: a reviewer could ask why exact methods are not used at that size.

papers.citation: Wenqian Jiang, Chenye Wu. "Deciphering convex hull pricing: effectively aligning demand with electricity prices enabled by approximated Minkowski sum." Electric Power Systems Research 262 (2027 issue) 113675. DOI 10.1016/j.epsr.2026.113675.
papers.what_they_do: Only the bibliographic record is verified, via Crossref; it has no abstract, and the publisher page returned 403. A search-engine summary says the paper builds an offline mapping from demand-space partitions to convex-hull prices for fast lookup, using an inner approximation of polytope Minkowski sums. That content is not verified.
papers.overlap_with_egg: If the summary is accurate, this is the nearest adjacent work: data-driven or precomputed convex-hull prices for UC. It is not a learned primal heuristic, and it does not address EV fleets.

papers.citation: Armando Teles Dauer, Bruno de Athayde Prata. "Variable fixing heuristics for solving multiple depot vehicle scheduling problem with heterogeneous fleet and time windows." Optimization Letters 15(1):153-170 (online 2020-04-06). DOI 10.1007/s11590-020-01577-0.
papers.what_they_do: Only the bibliographic record is verified, via Crossref, which carries no abstract. Gerbaux et al. (§2.4) describe it as using 'a supervised approach' to reduce the number of variables on a time-space MDVSP network. I did not verify that content independently.
papers.overlap_with_egg: Earlier supervised variable reduction for (non-electric) vehicle scheduling, predating Gerbaux. It further erodes 'learned reduction for bus scheduling' as a novelty claim.

what_remains_novel_for_egg: NOT novel (do not claim): learned or GNN/attention arc scoring by imitation of incumbents for electric bus scheduling (Gerbaux 2025); keeping the top-m incoming and outgoing arcs per trip (Gerbaux Algorithm 2, which is essentially EGG's E10 rule); a global keep fraction for learned network reduction (Morabit 2023); greedy-plus-learned hybrid keep sets (Gerbaux §5.3); transfer to larger instances (Gerbaux reaches 2374-3115 trips, beyond EGG's largest public case of 105 services); predict-and-fix and trust-region correction (Han 2023, ConPaS 2024, Apollo 2025), including for EV routing and charging MIPs (Yap 2025); learned dual or Lagrangian warm starts and learned stabilization for CG (Sugishita 2024, Demelas 2024, Shen 2024, Sarkar 2025, Wang and Khir 2026, You et al. 2026); and seeding the restricted master problem with columns (Sugishita's 'column pre-population' baseline, which is E9's mechanism).

Plausibly new, within the limits of this search: price-coupled learned pruning. EGG's MILP objective includes time-varying electricity prices and a quadratic aggregate supply cost that couples all buses' charging, and its scorer uses window-price features. Gerbaux's cost has no energy price (Table 1 has c_F, c_W, deadhead, c_R, c_H only) and its features contain no price (Table B.7). This is a modeling difference, not yet a demonstrated benefit: E7 tariff-aware scores were worse on all 6 public cells (GPT_HANDOFF_20261002.md line 41).

Plausibly new: tariff-induced distribution shift as a learning problem for bus scheduling. Gerbaux varies depots, stations and depot returns, not prices. E1 shows topology changes in 14/16 timetables with the tariff, and E4 trains across 7 tariffs. ConPaS-style solution pools are generic, but the tariff-shift question for fleet topology was not found in prior art.

Plausibly new: the target object, a certified complete-fleet convex-hull price-support statement for an electric bus fleet (does a uniform price exist that supports the physical fleet optimum, and how large is the physical-minus-hull gap: E0, 4/16 certified positive gaps). Learned primal search feeds this object, but stays independent of prediction accuracy. Across four targeted searches I found no paper combining learned primal heuristics with convex-hull-price certification, and none computing convex-hull prices for an EV or bus fleet as a single coupled participant. That is a search result, not a novelty proof. The mechanism (seed columns, learned duals) is not new; only the economic object and its EV-fleet coupling are candidates.

A variant, not a contribution: pruning a compact path-flow MILP with continuous time-indexed charging under shared capacity, solved directly by Gurobi with four tangent supply-cost rounds and gated by exact event replay. Gerbaux instead prunes the SPPRC pricing networks inside a CG diving heuristic. This matters for the comparison, but it does not by itself make EGG original.

A potential OR contribution, still unbuilt: a budget-allocation policy between learned primal search and unrestricted certifying pricing for a single hard coupled oracle, with a guarantee beyond Wang and Khir's (2026) stabilization bounds or You et al.'s (2026) no-bound-loss recovery. It would also need a fleet-specific safe-screening or bound-reuse result that existing inexact or stabilized CG does not give.
prior_art.implication:
I checked GPT's review against primary sources, and its main novelty warning holds. I read Gerbaux et al. (Computers & Operations Research 173, 2025, 106848, DOI 10.1016/j.cor.2024.106848) in full from the published PDF. Its bibliographic details, the figures of 71.6% time reduction and +2.2% cost over 405 instances of 568-1474 trips, the per-trip incoming/outgoing top-n_A rule (Algorithm 2) and the greedy-plus-GNN hybrid (§5.3) all match GPT's account. I read Sugishita, Grothey and McKinnon (INFORMS Journal on Computing 36(4):1129-1146, 2024, DOI 10.1287/ijoc.2022.0140) in full from the arXiv v2 manuscript, and its citation is also correct.

GPT understated three points:
(1) EGG's E10 rule is essentially Gerbaux's Algorithm 2 (/Users/nadan/Documents/ChatGPT/egg/claude-research-20261001/research-20261001/e10-per-trip/E10_RESULTS.md line 4; PROTOCOL.md line 6).
(2) Gerbaux was funded by GIRO Inc. EGG's sealed data include private GIRO data, so the closest prior art comes from the same industrial ecosystem, and reviewers will know it.
(3) Sugishita's 'column pre-population' baseline is exactly E9's mechanism of seeding hull CG with learned plans. Learned duals beat it at tight tolerance on the 600- and 1000-generator instances (1000 generators at 0.25%: 112.6 s for pre-population vs 65.9 s for the double-sampling network). Sugishita's D-W bound is the convex-hull (Lagrangian) relaxation, so learned warm starts for convex-hull computation are published even though the paper never says 'convex hull pricing'.

The 2024-2026 searches add more crowding:
- EV predict-and-fix exists (Yap et al. 2025, IJCNN per arXiv comments).
- Learned duals and stabilization for CG are an active line (Demelas ICML 2024, Shen ICML 2024, Sarkar CIE 2025, Wang and Khir 2026, You et al. 2026). You et al. even provide a recovery procedure with no bound loss.
- No paper combining learned primal heuristics with convex-hull-price certification was found, and none computing convex-hull prices for an EV fleet. That is a search result, not proof.

Consequences:
(a) EGG must drop any claim of a first GNN/learned electric-bus pruning, per-trip top-m, or learned convex-hull warm start. It should present ML as the enabling tool for the economic contribution: certified price support for a price-coupled EV fleet, plus the tariff-shift question.
(b) Before any further ML claim, add Gerbaux's baselines on EGG cases: the greedy-plus-learned union (cgHBD-style), a random keep set of the same size (cgRND), and the oracle 'utopic' keep set (labels from the reference solution) to bound the attainable speedup. Gerbaux shows learned-only keep sets can be catastrophic at small n_A (+161.3% for cgGNN(A,1)), which mirrors E10's m=3 results (+18.5% on Hildenbrand 16, +24.6% on Eberbach).
(c) For the hull work (Protocol 3), add Sugishita-style learned-dual warm starts with regularization, and column pre-population, as explicit baselines against EGG's seeded columns, with end-to-end time.
(d) Gerbaux's public MDEVSP instances (gerad.ca/~guyd/mdevsp.html, up to about 3000 trips) are a ready head-to-head benchmark. EGG would first need a model mapping: piecewise charging, 15-min periods, depot returns, and no energy price.
(e) Scale is EGG's weakest axis relative to the prior art (105 services vs 2600 trips).

Verification granularity: Gerbaux and Sugishita were read in full. Morabit (both papers), Han, ConPaS, Apollo, Demelas, Shen, Tanneau and Van Hentenryck, Yap, Wang and Khir, You et al., Abouelrous and Haslinger were checked against primary abstract or bibliographic records only. Sarkar, Jiang and Wu, and Dauer and Prata are verified only as Crossref bibliographic records; their content is unverified.

root_cause_hypotheses: PRIMARY (directly evidenced on one archived incumbent, case 10037): integrality-tolerance trickle flow through continuous-binary linking rows. The model encodes 'movement off => no charge' as z <= cap*x (native_pathflow.py:190) and 'movement on => SOC balance' as big-M rows with M = B+energy (native_pathflow.py:196, 205-206, 210, 217-218). python-mip's default integer_tol = 1e-6 is passed to Gurobi IntFeasTol (mip/gurobi.py:668-669) and is never overridden in egglab. Gurobi therefore returns binaries at delta or 1-delta with delta <= 1e-6 (observed 2.2816e-07), and the LP actively exploits them: z = cap*delta on the 'off' twin and SOC residual up to M*delta on the 'on' twins. Extraction rounds x at 0.5 (native_pathflow.py:356) but keeps the continuous values solved for the fractional x ('round-then-reuse' instead of 'round-then-re-solve').

The five messages are mainly two gates catching that one event. If the near-0 twin carries charge, the orphan ledger trips first (native_pathflow.py:347). If it carries none (e.g., a direct movement), the SOC residual reaches replay (native_recharge.py:342/345). Demonstrated: zeroing the 1.8481e-05 kWh orphan on the 10037 incumbent converts 'charge projection exceeds roundoff budget' into 'Used bus did not finish fully replenished'. Loosening the 1e-8 budget therefore cannot fix the problem, and GPT's note is right to forbid loosening replay.

Calibration mismatch: the 1e-8 kWh budget was designed (doc/NATIVE_PATHFLOW_ORPHAN_CHARGE_REPAIR_DESIGN_20260927.md) around a CBC artifact with x exactly 0.0 and an orphan of 1.2214110437041203e-12 kWh, which is FeasibilityTol scale. The real Gurobi mechanism is IntFeasTol scale, 1e-6 * caps up to 8.81e+03 kWh, 3 to 6 orders of magnitude larger. Tuning tolerances cannot close the gap. Even Gurobi's minimum IntFeasTol of 1e-9 leaves orphans up to 8.81e-06 kWh on Eberbach (881x budget), although it would bring the per-movement SOC slack (6.25e-07) under ENERGY_TOL 1e-6.

SECONDARY (inferred; no incumbents archived): one fleet-wide 1e-8 L1 budget versus FeasibilityTol 1e-8 per row, over many saturated interval-capacity rows. The prior N+O is charged first, and I and J double-count capacity excess at native_pathflow.py:386. This explains 'Combined negative correction/capacity excess exceeds' (native_recharge.py:577) and 'charge/decoding correction exceeds' (native_pathflow.py:393).

AMPLIFIER: all-or-nothing error handling (native_pathflow.py:592/537, native_hull.py:870 with the catch list at :961-969) turns any single bad incumbent into the loss of every earlier replay-valid plan and bound. More tangent rounds, pricing calls and long budgets mean more draws.

Failures depend on the solver path and are not deterministic. Scaling is not the driver. Binaries must stay in {0,1}, and the trickle magnitude cap*delta is in kWh whatever the continuous rescaling. Coefficients in the relevant rows run from about 0.9 (eta) to 624.6 (M), with caps up to 360 kWh, which is moderate. NumericFocus and scaling address the secondary FeasibilityTol mechanism, not the primary one.

Method 2: the route relaxation with a certified global reduced-cost floor rho over the entire optimistic route universe, artificial routes included, and the outward-enclosed corrected bound.
No price adaptation, no cross-method incumbents, no outer hull loop.

Three fixed price vectors per case, e.g. 'day' a, flat, and a signed variant with negative-price hours, inside the registered domain. Three paired seeds.
